name: sWARm
description: Personal project aimed at analyzing and projecting baseball player performance. It calculates metrics similar to fWAR and bWAR, employing data parsing and traditional machine learning algorithms to assess player value.
detailed_description: sWARm is a Python-based project that analyzes baseball player performance using data from sources like Baseball Savant, Fangraphs and other reputable sources. It attempts to calculate an equivalent to the industry standard WARP/fWAR and employs a variety of machine learning algorithms ranging from basic linear regression to a neural net to project future performance. The project utilizes libraries such as Pandas for data manipulation, scikit-learn and Keras for machine learning, and Plotly for data visualization.
problemStatement: Publicly available WAR figures (fWAR, bWAR) are computed by proprietary, closed-source models, making it hard to understand or reproduce how a player's value is actually calculated.
result: Currently benchmarking a progression of models, from linear regression through a neural network, against public fWAR/bWAR figures; project is ongoing and not yet finalized.
implementationDetails: Pulls and parses player performance data from Baseball Savant and Fangraphs.
Builds progressively complex models (linear regression, scikit-learn estimators, and a Keras neural net) to approximate WAR-equivalent player value.
Visualizes projections and model comparisons with Plotly.

name: Scentinel
description: Based off of recent cologne wear, season, and notes in cologne -> suggest a variety of colognes from current collection to potentially wear
detailed_description: Scentinel is a machine learning project that recommends colognes based on recent wear patterns, seasonal trends, and fragrance notes. Built using Python and Scikit Learn, it leverages collaborative filtering and content-based filtering techniques to provide personalized fragrance suggestions. The project utilizes a dataset of cologne attributes and user preferences to train the recommendation model.
problemStatement: Deciding which cologne to wear from a growing personal collection, based on season and recent rotation, was entirely ad hoc.
result: Built a working recommendation model combining collaborative and content-based filtering over a personal fragrance dataset, served through a FastAPI backend.
implementationDetails: Trains collaborative and content-based filtering models in scikit-learn over fragrance notes, season, and wear history.
Serves recommendations through a FastAPI backend backed by SQL storage.

name: GridironMetrics
description: A from-scratch, context-aware evaluation system for NFL offensive skill players, built to test whether independent methodology converges with industry-standard grading like PFF, and where it diverges, why.
detailed_description: GridironMetrics evaluates NFL offensive skill players (QB/RB/WR/TE) through a multi-phase contextual adjustment pipeline built on Polars, weighting every play by 10+ factors including field position, coverage type, personnel groupings, and weather. It's enriched with NextGen Stats GPS tracking and FTN human-charted flags (contested catches, play action, blitz recognition) specifically to separate player skill from scheme or situation using objective, verifiable flags rather than subjective, human-assigned grades. A supplementary scikit-learn ensemble handles player-props projections on top of the core rankings.
problemStatement: Whether an independently-built, objective-flag-based evaluation system for offensive skill players would converge with established, subjectively-graded industry consensus like PFF, and where it didn't, what specifically explained the gap.
result: For 2025 wide receivers, the system's top 4 exactly matched PFF's post-season top 4 (Nacua, Smith-Njigba, St. Brown, Chase), just reordered. The clearest divergence: players with injury-shortened seasons (Drake London, Christian Watson, Terry McLaurin) ranked far lower here than in PFF's grades, because this system sums contribution cumulatively across games played while PFF grades per-snap quality independent of games missed — a real methodological difference, not an error in either system.
implementationDetails: Multi-phase contextual adjustment pipeline (field position, score differential, down and distance, coverage type, personnel groupings, weather) applied to play-by-play data via Polars.

Integrates NextGen Stats GPS tracking (pressure, separation) and FTN charting (contested catches, play action, blitz, true drops) to adjust for scheme and situation using objective flags instead of subjective grading.
Position-specific adjustment logic for QB/RB/WR/TE, plus a supplementary scikit-learn ensemble for player-props projections.
Full season coverage from 2000 to present, with per-position rankings regenerated each year.

name: Unsub
description: A self-hosted Gmail unsubscriber that scans your inbox for newsletters and subscriptions, then sorts them by how they can actually be removed: one-click, email-based, web link, or unsupported.
detailed_description: Unsub connects to Gmail through OAuth and scans message headers to find every sender you're subscribed to, grouping them together and sorting by how recently they emailed you. Each sender is tagged by its unsubscribe method: RFC 8058 one-click, an email-based request sent through the Gmail API, a web link you handle manually, or unsupported if no unsubscribe header exists at all. It runs entirely on your own machine with your own OAuth credentials, only reads message metadata, and only requests send access for the mailto-based unsubscribes it needs to perform. A FastAPI backend handles the scanning and Gmail API calls, with a PostgreSQL database keeping track of senders and their status between runs.
problemStatement: Hunting down unsubscribe links across a cluttered inbox is tedious, and not every link is equally trustworthy: some are genuinely one-click, others quietly require a further confirmation step, and handing full inbox access to a third-party service to fix this raises its own privacy problem.
result: Built a working pipeline that scans a Gmail inbox via OAuth and classifies every sender by unsubscribe method, distinguishing RFC 8058 one-click-capable senders from lower-confidence mailto, link-only, or unsupported cases, with state persisted between runs so already-handled senders don't resurface.
implementationDetails: Scopes OAuth to gmail.metadata rather than full read access, so the app only ever sees message headers, never email content.
Detects RFC 8058 support (List-Unsubscribe-Post) to identify senders that can be unsubscribed with a single POST request and no further redirects.
FastAPI backend handles Gmail API scanning and unsubscribe actions, rendered through server-side Jinja2 templates.
PostgreSQL tracks each sender's classification and unsubscribe status across runs.
